cards.0635: A woman who clears houses for a living is in a garage off a road behind the parade on a Monday morning taking out what a lad she is working with says to take out, and one of the things is a folding chair with a split leg, and she has decided before she gets there that she is taking it whether it is on the list or not. She mends the leg on her own back step in the afternoon with a bracket off a shelf and a spanner. Nobody asked her and nobody is thanked and she has told nobody.
cards.0636: The chair is put down in a kitchen at number twelve on a Saturday morning and the woman there, who is in her late seventies, accepts it in about four seconds because she has been eating standing since before Christmas. That night she works out that accepting a thing means owing somebody, and she invents a false origin for it, and the false origin is a man who came for a fridge, and no man has ever come for a fridge at number twelve.
cards.0637: A man in his early forties who makes things has noticed the same woman eating standing on a gate twice and has decided to build her something. He builds a stool rather than a chair so that it cannot be confused with anything, and he builds it too heavy, which is the same mistake in a different shape, and a man at the bench with him asks him what it is for and he gives a reason that is not the reason.
cards.0638: The stool is carried up a path to number twelve on a Wednesday evening and put down in the same kitchen as the chair, and she says thank you in the only way she has, which is that it is nice that, and he cannot say where it came from, and the chapter is about what she does for the rest of that evening and the next morning with two things in a kitchen she had made do with one.
cards.0639: On a Saturday morning she is in a queue on the parade with her basket and a woman she does not know makes a joke in front of a man carrying a fridge about a man who came for her fridge, and a man standing behind her has heard the whole thing, and that man is the man who built the stool, and he says nothing, and goes home, and has now got a thing he cannot ask about and will not ask about.
cards.0640: The woman who brought the chair goes back to number twelve on a Friday with a spanner because the chair has started to slip, and finds the stool, and does not say anything about it, and mends a leg on a stool that is not hers, and is given a false origin for it by the woman she brought the chair to, who is protecting the man and not her, and she accepts the protection, and cannot be got at afterwards. THE FIRST FALSE ORIGIN FOR THE STOOL, NOT A SECOND, AND THE FILE SAID SECOND AND THE CHAPTER WON.
cards.0641: The woman at number twelve stands on the folding chair to get a tin down off a high cupboard and it goes over, and both of the two people who have been coming to that kitchen are there inside an hour of each other, and neither of them can be got out of the room, and they look at each other, and neither asks the other anything, and she lies twice in one afternoon to keep them in separate rooms, and it is the first time either of them has been told anything false about the other.
cards.0642: The two of them are alone on the Wednesday, without her, and they have a conversation in which they agree on exactly one thing and the thing they agree on is wrong, which is that they will both keep on coming and will not tell her they have met.
cards.0643: The woman at number twelve decides on the Monday that she is going to stop moving one chair and not the other twice a day, and she stops, and she does it by putting the stool on the step at number nine, where a woman in her late fifties also eats standing and has never been spoken to by either of them.
cards.0644: The woman who brought the chair finds the stool on the step at number nine and goes back to number twelve, and to keep the woman there out of it, tells her that the man who came for the fridge did come, and that there is a card, and that the card had nothing ticked on it, and the woman at number twelve looks at her and does not say anything, and then asks her for one thing, and the chapter ends on the asking.
